title: Graffiti: So Cool It’s A Pillar of Hip Hop
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and culture of graffiti, from precursors like Mexican muralism and Chicano writing through the 1960s-70s New York origins (Cornbread, Taki 183, Writers Corner 188), the three styles (tags, throw-ups, pieces) plus wild style, solo style and anti/ignorant style, tools and paint history (spray can invention, markers, Rustoleum/Krylon, lead paint, nozzles), the five pillars of hip hop, von Bode and Cheech Wizard influence, Style Wars and other documentaries, legal crackdowns in New York (Lindsay, Koch, Clean Car program), reverse graffiti and handstyle tips, famous artists (Basquiat, Keith Haring, Shepard Fairey, Lady Pink, Futura and Dondi White's "Break"), and a listener email correcting a Letterman/Leno fact.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the graffiti episode and tease wild style and a possible middle-aged-dude moment.

segments.title: Precursors to graffiti
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss early precursors such as Mexican muralism in the 1930s and Chicano kids' writing in LA, which used paint and brushes to tag neighborhoods.

segments.title: Spray can and markers
segments.summary: The spray can is credited to 1949 invention by Illinois paint company owner Ed Seymour and his wife Bonnie while trying to coat radiators; markers came later, with Magic Marker sold commercially from 1953.

segments.title: Cornbread and early New York tags
segments.summary: Darryl McCrae, known as Cornbread, is described as an early writer starting in 1965 in Philly; early Spanish Harlem tags such as Julio 204 and Taki 183 are mentioned.

segments.title: Taki 183 and Writers Corner 188
segments.summary: Taki 183 was covered by a 1971 New York Times article; the same year the crew WC 188 formed at Audubon Avenue and 188th Street to share style tips.

segments.title: Subway graffiti and risk
segments.summary: Graffiti moved onto subway cars, painted in rail yards at night; risk was part of the appeal, and crackdowns made it more challenging.

segments.title: Break before styles
segments.summary: Brief transition in which the hosts agree to break down the styles before a break.

segments.title: Tags, throw-ups, pieces and wild style
segments.summary: The three categories of graffiti are tags, throw-ups, and pieces, with time investments ranging from minutes to months; wild style is described as the most intricate, nearly illegible form, and its guidelines were set in the 1970s in New York.

segments.title: Solo style and anti style
segments.summary: Solo style, a West Coast Chicano lettering style with cartoon gangbanger characters, is described, along with anti or ignorant style, a deliberately primitive style.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Sponsor and ad break.

segments.title: Graffiti tools and the five pillars of hip hop
segments.summary: Early markers such as Pilot, Dry Mark, and Sanford King Size were used and refilled; artists made their own tools. Graffiti is one of the hip hop pillars, along with MCing, DJing, breaking and knowledge; graffiti has competitive spraying over others.

segments.title: Vaughn Bode and Cheech Wizard
segments.summary: Comic artist Vaughn Bode's characters Cheech Wizard and Puck the Lizard appeared in graffiti; the hosts link Bode to bubble lettering and the Beastie Boys song Sure Shot.

segments.title: Spread of graffiti worldwide
segments.summary: Graffiti spread to Britain and Amsterdam's punk scene in the late seventies.

segments.title: Documentaries and photographers
segments.summary: Henry Chalfant and Tony Silver made Style Wars (1983), and Chalfant worked on Subway Art with Martha Cooper and Spray Can Art with James Prigoff; Gordon Matta-Clark's photographs of tags are mentioned.

segments.title: Wild Style film
segments.summary: The 1982 film Wild Style, considered the first hip hop movie, featured Lady Pink, Rock City Crew, and King Ad-Rock.

segments.title: Graffiti goes to the art world
segments.summary: Hugo Martinez started United Graffiti Artists in 1972; the group had a City College exhibition and a SoHo gallery show, and Twyla Tharp used their work for a 1973 dance performance.

segments.title: Crackdowns in New York
segments.summary: Mayor John Lindsay declared war on graffiti; the city banned carrying aerosol cans in public facilities and created a Transit Police Graffiti Squad; Ed Koch used razor wire, guard dogs and surveillance; the Clean Car program cleaned cars before they left the yard.

segments.title: Break by Dondi and Futura 2000
segments.summary: The full subway car piece Break by Dondi and Futura 2000 is described as a landmark; Chuck and Josh discuss their reactions.

segments.title: Spray paint brands, lead and nozzles
segments.summary: Rust-Oleum and Krylon avoided marketing to graffiti artists, though artists used them; lead made paint dry faster and brighter until it was removed in the late seventies; European brands Montana and Molotov targeted street art; caps like needle and calligraphy caps.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Sponsor and ad break.

segments.title: Learning graffiti: handstyle and technique
segments.summary: Beginners should develop a handstyle with pens and markers; Bombing Science lists alphabets of 61 artists; tips include shaking the can, controlling pressure and distance from the wall; codes of conduct include not tagging churches, schools, hospitals, homes, cemeteries or nature, and not snitching.

segments.title: Other forms: stickers, stencils, reverse graffiti
segments.summary: Other graffiti forms include wheat paste posters, stickers, and stencils; reverse graffiti cleans dirt to create images, such as writing in dusty cars.

segments.title: Graffiti artists who became famous
segments.summary: Jean-Michel Basquiat (tag SAMO, with Al Diaz) had a 1982 solo show; Keith Haring's Radiant Baby, Basquiat's death from heroin, and Haring's death from AIDS-related complications are discussed; Shepard Fairey's Andre the Giant and Obama Hope posters.

segments.title: More artists
segments.summary: Hosts mention Dondi White, Lady Pink, REN s in Copenhagen, Kid Acne/kid Olt who vandalizes luxury brand stores, and Apothecary, the tag of Umi, which was too long to use.

segments.title: Listener mail: Letterman and Leno
segments.summary: Ben from Connecticut notes David Letterman co-owns Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing, which won the Indy 500 in 2004 and 2020, correcting a joke about Leno and cars from the Selects episode about the Wendy's chili finger.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Show credits and iHeartRadio outro.
